cover.alt: Helga looks back from a boat as emigrants leave Seyðisfjörður.
cover.art_brief: Ink and watercolour in the established Kvöldvakan style, fully clothed 1876 Icelandic travellers. Seyðisfjörður harbour at about ten in the evening on 12 July, a pale summer night. A large black steamer at anchor gives off smoke. Small rowing boats carry emigrants and their travelling chests toward it. Helga sits in the third boat with three women from other farms, looking back at the shore and waving. On the shore Siggi waves his cap; Guðrún and afi with Ásta remain there. Jón has three chests and Ketill carries two bags; Lilja goes with her mother. Show these with their party, without assigning a boat number to them. No Bjarni at the harbour, no modern objects, no lettering, no invented flag or ship markings. Planned only; the prose supplies every lexical inference.

inference_aids.alt: Bjarni remains beside the farmhouse wall while the others ride away from Hamrar.
inference_aids.art_brief: Ink and watercolour, Hamrar on a July morning in 1876, the established turf farmhouse and farm dress. From the mountain path Siggi looks down at Bjarni, alone and still by the farmhouse wall in the yard. Helga, Guðrún, afi, Siggi and Ásta ride away on horses, with Helga’s travelling chest on one horse; Ásta rides with afi. Bjarni stays at home. Do not show the party walking or Bjarni waving; Helga waves in the next segment. No lettering or modern equipment. Match the frozen riding scene; planned only, no lexical support.

Óli fór fyrstur í bátinn, og Jón kom á eftir honum með þrjár kistur. Ketill bar tvo poka, og Lilja fór með móður sinni. Helga sat í þriðja bátnum, hjá þremur konum frá öðrum bæjum.

inference_aids.gloss: í þriðja bátnum: í báti 3

segments.text: Bátarnir fóru hægt út á fjörðinn. Helga horfði á ströndina og veifaði. Siggi veifaði húfunni sinni.

inference_aids.alt: Helga looks back from a boat as emigrants leave Seyðisfjörður.
inference_aids.art_brief: Ink and watercolour in the established Kvöldvakan style, fully clothed 1876 Icelandic travellers. Seyðisfjörður harbour at about ten in the evening on 12 July, a pale summer night. A large black steamer at anchor gives off smoke. Small rowing boats carry emigrants and their travelling chests toward it. Helga sits in the third boat with three women from other farms, looking back at the shore and waving. On the shore Siggi waves his cap; Guðrún and afi with Ásta remain there. Jón has three chests and Ketill carries two bags; Lilja goes with her mother. Show these with their party, without assigning a boat number to them. No Bjarni at the harbour, no modern objects, no lettering, no invented flag or ship markings. Planned only; the prose supplies every lexical inference.

segments.text: Klukkan tólf sigldi skipið. Svartur reykur kom upp úr því, og það fór hægt út fjörðinn.

words_with_history.title: Orð með sögu
text: Afi sagði frá Gimli í Völuspá. Eftir ragnarök sá gamla konan höll. Þakið var úr gulli. Höllin var fögur, og sólin var ekki eins fögur. Þar bjuggu góðir menn.
Ketill talaði um bæ í Kanada. Menn frá Íslandi komu þangað árið átján hundruð sjötíu og fimm. Á leiðinni gáfu þeir bænum nafnið Gimli. Það var fyrsti íslenski bærinn í Kanada.
Helga sagði: „Þá fer ég á Gimli. Þar er framtíð mín.“ Hún talaði um bæinn, en afi talaði um höllina. Óli vildi fara strax, ekki eftir ragnarök. Sama nafnið fór með þeim vestur.
words_with_history.note_en: The history brief credits Ólafur Ólafsson frá Espihóli with choosing Gimli during the river journey in October 1875. Gimlé is the poem’s form of Gimli. The quotation follows Netútgáfan, Völuspá 65, incipit “Sal sér hún standa”, with gulli þaktan. The research brief’s 64 belongs to another numbering convention.

Mér líður bæði vel og illa (s035); Mér líkar ekki reykurinn (s047); henni leist vel á það (s046); Mér þykir það fallegt nafn (s090)

grammar.note_en:
Numbers one to four change form to agree with the noun’s gender and case. Gender is the noun’s grammatical class: masculine (kk.), feminine (kvk.) or neuter (hk.). Case shows its role in the sentence: nominative (nf.) commonly marks a subject or predicate, accusative (þf.) an object, dative (þgf.) certain objects or the phrase after a preposition, and genitive (ef.) possession or a measure. The first table shows every case of one, two, three and four. Segment references identify the forms actually read in the story. The one cell marked † is reference only: masculine nominative þrír does not occur in this chapter and is not a drill answer. The table mixes attested genders rather than silently supplying a full three-gender paradigm. Headwords identify the words; they do not claim that every citation form occurs in the story.

Eitt pund (s007) means “one pound”: pund is neuter. Eina ferð (s010), “one journey”, is feminine accusative; einn farþega (s011), “one passenger”, is masculine accusative. Á einum þeirra (s021), “on one of them”, refers to a horse, and í einum hópnum (s054), “in one of the groups”, is also masculine dative. Einu ári (s081), “one year”, is neuter dative. Hann var alveg einn (s031), “he was all alone”, uses nominative masculine einn without a following noun; it does not mean he was one year old.

Tveir mánuðir (s079) means “two months”, masculine nominative in the sentence “The journey is nearly two months”. Tveimur vikum (s003), “two weeks”, is dative feminine; tveimur börnum (s060), “two children”, is dative neuter; tveimur árum (s067), “two years”, is also dative neuter. The numeral’s dative form tveimur works with all three genders. Tveggja daga ferð (s017) means “a two-day journey”: the measure “of two days” is genitive. Þrjár, “three”, agrees with feminine sheep in s003 and chests in s107, both accusative; hjá þremur konum (s107), “beside three women”, is dative after hjá. Þau eru fjögur (s011), “there are four of them”, uses neuter for the mixed family group. Fjögur hundruð (s050) means “four hundred”, with neuter plural hundruð. Fyrir fjóra (s011), “for four [people]”, has masculine accusative fjóra standing without its noun. The reference nominative þrír is explicitly marked †; it is not an additional production target.

The revised registration and boarding scenes complete the case contrasts. Eins farþega (s057), “of one passenger”, is masculine genitive: Fargjald eins farþega means “the fare of one passenger”. Þriggja kinda (s013), “of three sheep”, is feminine genitive in verð þriggja kinda, “the price of three sheep”. Fjögurra manna fjölskylda (s060) means “a family of four people”; fjögurra manna is genitive. The genitive forms tveggja, þriggja and fjögurra are the same in all three genders. Eins in eins farþega is masculine genitive; einn does not have the same genitive form in every gender. Á fjórum dögum (s061), “in four days”, is a dative duration: the ship will make the Scotland leg in that time. It is distinct from fyrir tveimur árum, “two years ago”. Ketill bar tvo poka (s107), “Ketill carried two bags”, supplies masculine accusative tvo. Compare all four forms of two: tveir mánuðir (nominative), tvo poka (accusative), tveimur börnum (dative), tveggja daga ferð (genitive). Pensa A practises that contrast only after all four have been read.

An ordinal places something in a sequence: first, second, third. Frá fyrsta degi (s083) means “from the first day”; á öðrum degi (s042), “on the second day”; í þriðja bátnum (s107), “in the third boat”. These are dative phrases. Óli fór fyrstur í bátinn (s107), “Óli was the first to get into the boat”, uses strong masculine nominative fyrstur, agreeing with Óli. Do not substitute fyrsta in that frame. Tólfta júlí (s016) means “on the twelfth of July”: the date uses an accusative ordinal with the month name. The contract prints 12. júlí 1876 (s015); the dot marks the ordinal date. Átján hundruð sjötíu og sex (s016) reads the year 1876 as “eighteen hundred and seventy-six”. Digits are allowed in the contract; the narration and spoken reading use words.

Fyrir takes different cases for different meanings. Fyrir tveimur vikum (s003), “two weeks ago”, fyrir tveimur árum (s067), “two years ago”, and fyrir næstum einu ári (s081), “nearly a year ago”, use dative for an interval before the current reference point. In past narration that point is the story’s time, not today. Contrast fyrir eina ferð (s010), “for one journey”, fyrir einn farþega (s011), “for one passenger”, and Jón borgar fyrir fjóra (s011), “Jón pays for four”: these use accusative for what or whom the payment covers. The ending and meaning work together; fyrir does not always mean “ago”.

Sex pund og níu skildinga (s005), “six pounds and nine shillings”, answers “What does the journey cost?” with an accusative amount. The masculine plural ending -a in skildinga differs from nominative skildingar in Tuttugu skildingar eru eitt pund (s007), “Twenty shillings are one pound”. Pund has the same visible spelling in these two uses. Sex and níu do not take case endings here. The contract label Fargjald: 6 pund 9 skildingar (s015), “Fare: £6 9s”, is a nominal label, not an accusative object sentence. £6 9s is 129 shillings; it does not mean £6.09. The chapter does not establish whether a child’s fare differed from an adult’s.

Age is expressed with a genitive measure: Ég er sjötíu og fimm vetra (s094), “I am seventy-five years old”, literally “of seventy-five winters”; Siggi var tólf vetra (s100), “Siggi was twelve years old”. Vetra is genitive plural of vetur. Ketill var einum vetri eldri (s100), “Ketill was one year older”, instead uses dative einum vetri for the amount of difference. Eldri is an already supported comparison word, not a new comparative paradigm. Clock time uses klukkan plus a number: klukkan tíu í kvöld (s061), “at ten this evening”, and klukkan tólf siglir skipið (s061), “at twelve the ship sails”. In this scene those are 22:00 and midnight. Marga tíma (s064), “many hours”, measures how long they waited, rather than naming a clock reading. Tveir mánuðir (s079), “two months”, names a duration in the nominative predicate of “the journey is …”.

The last table recalls the Hluti 2 verb system using this chapter’s attested forms. Var/voru (s001/s048) mean “was/were”; hafði (s020) means “had”. No unattested plural of hafa is supplied. In the weak past, the dental consonant d, ð or t belongs to the past formation. Veifaði (s032), “waved”, represents the -aði class and keeps a before ði. Horfði (s031), “looked”, supplies -ði. Fylgdi (s056), “followed”, has -di, not -ði. Telja → taldi (s002), “counted”, changes e to a and loses j. Selja → seldi (s003), “sold”, retains e and loses j; it does not change its stem vowel. Sigldi (s109), “sailed”, and kenndi (s103), “taught”, also have -di; staðfesti (s055), “confirmed”, ends in -ti. Borgaðir þú allt? (s057) means “Did you pay everything?”: borgaðir is second-person singular past, addressing Helga, with -r after the -aði formation. It is not an imperative or a supine. Learn each verb’s actual form rather than assuming every written stem stays unchanged.

Strong verbs use inherited stem patterns rather than a dental past suffix. Fór/fóru (s018/s022), “went” singular/plural, and kom/komu (s060/s042), “came” singular/plural, show the third-person plural -u. Riðu (s030), “rode”, and reru (s095), “rowed”, are plural past forms; their singulars are not tabulated because this chapter does not use them. Hvarf/hurfu (s110), “disappeared”, contrasts singular and plural with both a vowel change and the plural ending. Bar (s107), “carried”, is the strong singular past of bera. No perfect tense or supine construction is taught here.

The imperative gives a direct instruction to one person, often with the old þú clitic attached. Farðu (s028) means “go”; Gleymdu ekki nafninu mínu (s098), “Do not forget my name”; Skrifaðu mér um kindina (s105), “Write to me about the sheep”; Kenndu mér að skrifa (s114), “Teach me to write”. Skrifaðu keeps the a before -ðu. Trúðu mér (s041), “Trust me”, is the attested command of trúa: learn this form rather than keeping every infinitive’s final a mechanically. Other verbs have their own stem and consonant combinations, as in farðu, gleymdu and kenndu. Do not form every command merely by adding -ðu to the infinitive. Kenna takes a dative person: kenndi mér (s103), “taught me”, and kenndu mér (s114), “teach me”; að skrifa names the action taught.

Oblique subjects are experiencers in a case other than the ordinary nominative. Mér líður bæði vel og illa (s035), “I feel both good and bad”, and Mér líkar ekki reykurinn (s047), “I do not like the smoke”, use dative mér. Mig dreymdi einnig (s038), “I dreamt too”, uses accusative mig. The verb remains third-person singular in these frames even when the person means “I”. Case government belongs to the expression; the past tense dreymdi does not turn mig into mér.

The revised scene also recalls the past of lítast á: henni leist vel á það (s046), “she liked the look of it”. Henni is dative and refers to Helga; það is accusative and refers to the ship Verona. Leist is the past form in this existing oblique-subject expression. Mér þykir það fallegt nafn (s090) means “I think it is a beautiful name”: mér refers to Helga and það to the name Gimli. These do not introduce a general -st system before G24.
